name: Victor Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. Tell me about your morning at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor Young, forty-three, and I lead the small-business accounts team at a tax firm. This morning a bakery's sales looked healthy until I found the owner's cash drawings hidden under supplies; I enjoy giving someone a clear picture they can act on. I dislike sending a client another standard letter when a five-minute call would settle the question. I'm among the best accountants here, with a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I use AI tools every day for first drafts and sorting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does work have to support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Rosa works part-time at the library; our children are eight and eleven, and we have a mortgage. My pay is low for this senior team-lead job, we have less than a month's expenses saved, and there are few similar firms nearby. I'm comfortable trying a new tool or service, but I believe a business has to earn its keep and our family should cover its own costs when we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My week would look much the same. The firm has a little AI receipt sorter, but its errors still land on my desk before I sign the tax return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my staff to use the sorter and keep the client call with a person. I'd say the tool saves minutes, not the duty to explain a tax figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at spotting a bad assumption, but senior skill hasn't brought senior pay. My wife Rosa and I have a mortgage, children aged eight and eleven, and less than one month of expenses saved. There are few similar accounting firms near us, so even a steady market feels tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing accounts and tax returns, including my daily AI checks, and take our completed files to my next salary review. I'd ask for a written pay decision by the end of January. If they increase it, we'd put sixty a month into savings; if not, we'd drop the monthly cinema outing and keep our current wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, though not about a small sorter. I can find an error in a ledger faster than I can replace an empty savings month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill matters first this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son needs a new bicycle helmet, and the boiler inspection is due on the same payday. Rosa works part-time at the library and cannot add hours on demand. We'd buy the helmet and postpone the cinema; the inspection stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the salary review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the partners the return corrections I caught, not just a list of titles. My master's degree and chartered accountancy qualification got me to team lead, but the written pay figure is what matters at home. I will not budget on praise.

say: I would use the **receipt sorter** while a person checks each signed return.
I would keep a **client conversation** when a tax figure needs explaining.
think: My **low senior pay** limits what we can put aside.
Our **mortgage and children** make a thin reserve worrying already.
do: Continue **daily AI checks** and signed tax returns.
Seek a **written pay decision** by January.
Save **sixty monthly** after a raise; otherwise drop cinema outings.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our cash cushion.
S0.quote: I can find an error in a ledger faster than I can replace an empty savings month.
fieldNote: His **early AI use** is routine today and does not become a new learning action.
The **written raise** determines savings; otherwise the family keeps current wages and cuts a monthly outing.

steps.text: Keep preparing returns with daily AI checks
Save sixty monthly only after written pay rise
Drop monthly cinema outings if pay rise refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software writes letters and checks returns, a three-person tax team could become two. I'd start by measuring errors and client complaints rather than guessing whose chair goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the speed to win more small-business work and show our prices plainly. I'd also tell my team which paid hours the partners have actually guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose a paid review day if the fee per return falls. We have weeks of savings, and Rosa's library pay cannot carry the mortgage. I like trying new tools, but I can't gamble with the children's school routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a four-week AI draft trial on my own client letters and count corrections against time saved. Then I'd pitch one priced quarterly cash-flow call to existing clients, on paid firm time, only after a partner approves the fee. If my hours are cut, I'd apply for an advertised senior accounts role only with written mortgage-covering pay, start date and school pickup hours; if none fits, I'd stay on my paid rota while the firm still offers it and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my own paid day. An AI letter trial gives me information, not a guarantee of paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cash-flow call cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery owner asked last week why a profitable month still left a cash hole. A short paid call might answer that better than another automated letter. I'll ask the partner to approve a price before offering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a different job affect pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa collects our younger child on library days, but I collect both on Thursdays. I'd check a new role's closing time against that pickup and the cost of a club place. A verbal offer would not move us off a real payslip.

say: I would use **measured trials** to find errors and saved time.
I would pitch **priced cash-flow calls** only with approved paid hours.
think: My **paid review day** could disappear as fees fall.
Our **weeks of savings** cannot bridge an uncertain job search.
do: Run a **four-week letter trial** and count corrections.
Offer a **priced quarterly call** only with partner approval.
Apply after **hours cuts** only for written mortgage pay, start and pickup; otherwise keep offered paid hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost pay.
S1.quote: An AI letter trial gives me information, not a guarantee of paid work.
fieldNote: The **priced call** is a firm service, contingent on partner approval and paid time, not his own side business.
A **job move** requires an advertised post, written mortgage pay, start and workable pickup; he retains current paid hours otherwise.

steps.text: Run four-week AI letter trial and count corrections
Pitch priced client call only after partner approves fee and paid time
Apply after cut only to posted funded job with written mortgage pay, start and pickup
Keep offered paid rota hours if no suitable job opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 would reach tax preparation and my review work almost together. The robots around 2031 might change other jobs, but I'm already at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues to ask for written notice and a ledger of which services clients still pay for. I'd also tell my family that my first plan is to keep earning, even if the work title changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my post in the first year after 2028. The fact that I lead the team won't matter if clients buy the same thinking work cheaply. With less than a month saved, I would be frightened for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel our one-time holiday deposit of four hundred before it becomes non-refundable and hold it for bills. While still employed, I'd check posted payroll management vacancies at the hospital, though those desks also face AI. If my job ends after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd take a funded post only with written pay covering the mortgage, a confirmed start and pickup; without one I'd take any paid accounts hours the firm still offers and ask family for a short bridge with a repayment date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. AGI in 2028 is too close to turn our small reserve into a safe landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could anyone help with one payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and I would tell the children we are keeping the house plan simple. My brother could lend a little for one mortgage payment, but I would ask for an amount and repayment date rather than call it a solution. Rosa's library shifts are fixed, so the school pickup still has to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hospital has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital may have no funded vacancy, and I won't leave a current wage for a rumour. I'd keep filing any returns the firm still pays me to handle and search the posted openings each Friday. I would not count the 2031 robots as extra time for a tax desk.

say: I would seek **written notice** before desk posts end.
I would ask for **paid services**, not a new title alone.
think: My **tax post** may end in the first year after 2028.
A **weeks-long reserve** cannot cover the mortgage for long.
do: Hold the **one-time holiday deposit** for bills.
Check **posted hospital payroll jobs** now; after 2028 loss move only with funded mortgage pay, start and pickup.
Keep **offered paid accounts hours** and seek a dated family bridge if no vacancy opens.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected wage loss.
S2.quote: AGI in 2028 is too close to turn our small reserve into a safe landing.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** cannot protect a tax desk when AGI handles the same thinking work in 2028.
A **hospital vacancy** must be real and funded; family help is a short, dated bridge while he keeps paid work.

steps.text: Cancel one-time holiday deposit and hold four hundred for bills
Check posted funded hospital payroll jobs; move after loss with written mortgage pay, start and pickup
Keep offered paid accounts hours if no funded hospital vacancy opens
Ask brother for one-payment loan with dated repayment if job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to build a client service with a price instead of hoping a tax return stays scarce. AGI in 2031 would still take much of my screen work; the robots in 2034 aren't my deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses need a person who can ask why the owner keeps drawing cash. I'd tell the partners that the service only makes sense if the clients sign and our paid time is protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think two or three cash-flow clients might pay for a quarterly call, but that may not support my whole salary. I'm willing to test it early, yet I won't tell Rosa we are safe on a polite yes. The mortgage needs contracted income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd ask the partner to quote three existing clients a quarterly cash-flow review during paid hours. I'd build the worksheet with the AI tool I already use and proceed only if signed fees cover the hours. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if tax work ends, I'd keep contracted calls and any paid firm hours offered throughout applications for a posted funded finance lead job. I'd move only with written mortgage pay, a signed start date and school pickup; if no opening fits, I'd keep those paid hours while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer runway lets me test a fee with actual clients. A signed fee is a better forecast than a friendly nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a client agree to the price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery owner can tell me whether a quarterly review has a place in the budget. I would show the price on one page and ask for a signed booking. If the answer is no, I would not claim that conversation as future revenue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partner refuses paid pilot time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partner refuses paid time, I won't do the firm's client calls on evenings meant for my family. I'd keep my current returns and ask again at the next planning meeting with a smaller paid pilot. The client list belongs to the firm.

say: I would propose **priced cash-flow reviews** to existing clients.
I would require **signed fees** and protected paid hours first.
think: A **small client list** may not cover my whole salary.
Our **mortgage** needs contracted income, not friendly interest.
do: Quote **three quarterly reviews** next spring only during approved paid time and with signed covering fees.
Keep **contracted paid calls** and offered firm hours during the post-2031 search.
After **2031 tax loss**, move only for funded work with written mortgage pay, signed start and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** while testing a paid service.
S3.quote: A signed fee is a better forecast than a friendly nod.
fieldNote: The **client test** depends on partner approval and signed covering fees; refusal leaves him on current returns.
His **post-2031 search** requires funded vacancy, written mortgage pay, signed start and pickup; contracted calls and offered firm hours continue during applications.

steps.text: Quote three quarterly reviews only with approved paid time and signed covering fees
Keep contracted paid calls and offered firm hours during search
Apply after 2031 loss only for funded job with written mortgage pay, signed start and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets the children grow and lets me make a real savings habit if pay improves. AGI in 2036 still reaches our accounts and tax returns before robots turn up around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd argue for letting capable small firms compete on service, not for pretending software is forbidden. I'd also say families need time to make a plan while they are still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm more hopeful about building a cash-flow practice in ten years than in two. But we start with less than a month saved and a mortgage, and a long calendar does not add money by itself. The firm could still end my tax role after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the AI-assisted workflow I use daily and ask for a written senior pay rise this winter. Only if it arrives would we save sixty a month; otherwise we'd keep the present budget. Over the next two years I'd quote the cash-flow service to three clients with partner-approved paid time and continue it only if they sign fees covering my hours. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if tax work ends, I'd keep signed paid calls or take a funded finance role only after written mortgage pay, start and pickup are confirmed, while keeping any paid firm work offered if no vacancy fits and claiming support only if we qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current cash, although the decade gives me room to act. The mortgage is due monthly, not in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children help with the mortgage later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child could be grown by then, but I won't make the children's future earnings part of our payment plan. Rosa and I need the reserve from our own wages. A raise would go first to that, not a better car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if clients will not sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the clients won't sign, I won't launch a separate practice on debt. I'd keep the paid accounts work as long as the firm offers it and look at real vacancies before moving. I can be curious about software without betting the house on it.

say: I would let **small firms compete** through paid service.
I would ask for **time to plan** while wages continue.
think: A **ten-year runway** helps only if we build cash.
My **tax role** may still end when AGI arrives in 2036.
do: Save **sixty monthly** only after a written pay rise.
Quote **three cash-flow clients** with approved paid time and signed covering fees; keep contracted calls and offered firm hours.
After **2036 tax loss**, take funded work only with written wage, start and pickup; otherwise claim support if eligible.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our current thin reserve.
S4.quote: The mortgage is due monthly, not in ten years.
fieldNote: His **free-market outlook** supports competing through a paid service, while he refuses an unfunded private launch.
The **2036 decision** depends on signed fees or a funded vacancy with written mortgage pay, start and pickup.

steps.text: Save sixty monthly only after written senior pay rise
Quote three clients with approved paid time and signed covering fees; keep paid calls
Take funded role after 2036 loss only with written mortgage pay, start and pickup
Claim support if eligible and keep offered firm hours without a funded job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because tax preparation is screen work and my wage could go before we build even one month's reserve. The children need a steady house more than they need me to keep a particular title. Written notice, paid work through the change and a funded vacancy with a clear wage and start would help. A job title cannot make a mortgage payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the human call when software writes the answer. If a client will sign a fee, I'd try to build it. If not, the firm should say so before asking us to work for free.

headlineQuote: A job title cannot make a mortgage payment.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Victor leads small-business accounts and tax returns at a firm.
His **master’s** and chartered qualification match top skill, though his senior pay is low.
He uses **AI daily** for drafts and sorting and tests a priced cash-flow call.
Rosa’s **library pay**, two children, mortgage and less than one month saved make him cautious.
Few **local firms** mean a move needs written pay, start and school pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his desk wage before one month of savings exists.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written notice**, paid work and a funded opening with a clear wage and start.
